html:
The Hunger Winter was a famine in the German-occupied western Netherlands in the winter of 1944 to 1945. About 20,000 people died.

After the Allied failure at Arnhem in September 1944, the Dutch government in exile called a railway strike. The Germans answered with a ban on food transport to the west, and when it was eased, frozen canals stopped the barges. Rations in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague fell below 600 calories a day. People ate tulip bulbs and sugar beets.

Allied air drops of food and the liberation in May 1945 ended it. Studies of children born to mothers who starved during the famine became a famous source on how hunger in the womb affects health for life. It came in the last year of the occupation of the Netherlands in the Second World War, which also took the life of Anne Frank.
sum: The Hunger Winter was a famine in the German-occupied western Netherlands in the winter of 1944 to 1945. About 20,000 people died.
